## Architecture Vision Reference

Per [GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01 §Normative Language Convention](GUID-SEC-IAM-REF-2.2.01.md): **SHALL** = mandatory; **SHOULD** = strongly recommended; **MAY** = optional.

> **Standards Version**: This ABB references **NIST SP 800-63B** for authenticator assurance level (AAL) requirements. Implementing SBBs SHALL document the specific revision of NIST SP 800-63B in force at time of SBB design. Restricted authenticator treatment (SMS/voice OTP, §5.2.10) and phishing-resistant AAL3 requirements differ materially across revisions; the applicable revision SHALL govern restricted authenticator deprecation timelines and compensating control requirements.

[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-MFA-2.2.04.md#abb-scope]

### ABB Scope

**In Scope**:
- Authentication assurance level (AAL) architecture per NIST SP 800-63B
- Authenticator type classification and acceptable use policy (phishing-resistant, standard, restricted/deprecated)
- Phishing-resistant authenticator architecture (FIDO2/WebAuthn, PKI-based, hardware security keys)
- Adaptive and risk-based authentication architecture
- Authenticator lifecycle: enrollment, binding, renewal, revocation, and recovery
- Re-authentication triggers and session step-up requirements
- MFA enforcement for workforce, privileged users, and client-facing applications
- Legacy authenticator (SMS, voice OTP) deprecation path

**Out of Scope**:
- SSO session establishment and lifecycle (see GUID-SEC-IAM-SSO-2.2.03)
- Identity proofing prior to credential issuance (see GUID-SEC-IAM-PROOFING-2.2.05)
- Machine-to-machine authentication (see GUID-SEC-IAM-NON-HUMAN-AND-AI-STRATEGY-2.2.12)
- Physical access control and badge authentication
- Security controls, configuration requirements, and compliance mandates (belong in `standards/security/`)
- Solution Building Blocks and vendor product selection (Phase E–F)

[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-MFA-2.2.04.md#core-principles]

### Core Principles

**1. Universal MFA — No Exceptions Without Documented Risk Acceptance**

All interactive user authentication to enterprise systems, applications, and data SHALL require multifactor authentication. Single-factor authentication is prohibited for any system containing sensitive data or providing access to enterprise resources, regardless of network location. Exceptions SHALL require formal security risk acceptance with documented compensating controls and defined expiration dates.

**2. Phishing-Resistant Authenticators for Privileged and High-Sensitivity Access**

All privileged accounts, administrative interfaces, and access to high-sensitivity systems or data SHALL use phishing-resistant authenticators that provide verifier impersonation resistance. FIDO2/WebAuthn and PKI-based authenticators (hardware security keys, smart cards) meet this requirement. Push notification, TOTP, and authenticator app-based MFA do not provide phishing resistance and SHALL NOT be used as the sole factor for privileged access.

**3. Authentication Assurance Level Alignment**

MFA implementations SHALL align with NIST SP 800-63B Authentication Assurance Levels (AAL). AAL2 (multi-factor with approved authenticators) SHALL be the minimum baseline for all standard user access. AAL3 (hardware-bound phishing-resistant authenticator with verifier impersonation resistance) SHALL be required for privileged access, administrative operations, and high-risk transactions.

**4. Legacy Authenticator Deprecation**

SMS-based OTP and voice-call OTP are restricted authenticator types per NIST SP 800-63B and SHALL NOT be used for new implementations. Existing deployments using these factors SHALL have a documented deprecation plan with a defined timeline for migration to stronger authenticators. Email-based OTP SHOULD NOT be used as a primary MFA factor.

[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-MFA-2.2.04.md#authenticator-classification-and-policy]

#### Authenticator Classification and Policy

**Architectural intent**: Define a clear taxonomy of acceptable, restricted, and prohibited authenticator types mapped to assurance levels, providing a policy framework for consistent MFA implementation across the enterprise.

**Design guidance**:
- **Phishing-resistant authenticators (AAL3-capable)**: FIDO2/WebAuthn security keys (hardware-bound), platform authenticators (Windows Hello for Business, Touch ID, Face ID with TPM binding), PKI smart cards. SHALL be required for privileged access.
- **Standard authenticators (AAL2-capable)**: Mobile authenticator apps with push notification, Time-Based One-Time Password (TOTP) authenticator apps, hardware OTP tokens. MAY be used for standard workforce access.
- **Restricted authenticators (deprecated — not for new use)**: SMS OTP, voice call OTP, email OTP. SHALL have documented migration path; SHALL NOT be used for new implementations.
- The authenticator policy framework SHALL be maintained centrally and applied consistently across enterprise Identity Providers
page_texts.11:
[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-MFA-2.2.04.md#authenticator-lifecycle-management]

#### Authenticator Lifecycle Management

**Architectural intent**: Govern the full lifecycle of authenticators from enrollment through revocation, ensuring that authenticators are securely bound to verified identities and promptly revoked when no longer authorized.

**Design guidance**:
- Authenticator enrollment SHALL be bound to a verified identity; enrollment SHOULD require identity proofing commensurate with the authenticator's assurance level (per GUID-SEC-IAM-PROOFING-2.2.05)
- Self-service authenticator enrollment and recovery SHALL require identity re-verification at a level commensurate with the assurance level of the original enrollment, per GUID-SEC-IAM-PROOFING-2.2.05; recovery pathways that effectively downgrade the enrolled IAL or AAL are prohibited. Enrollment workflows SHALL NOT permit bypassing verification through helpdesk social engineering
- Authenticators SHALL be revoked upon user termination, role change requiring reduced access, authenticator loss, or security incident involving the authenticator
- Multiple authenticators SHOULD be registered per user to support recovery without reducing assurance level; recovery pathways SHALL NOT downgrade the effective AAL
page_texts.12:
[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-MFA-2.2.04.md#adaptive-and-risk-based-authentication]

#### Adaptive and Risk-Based Authentication

**Architectural intent**: Incorporate contextual signals into authentication decisions to apply appropriate authentication strength dynamically, enforcing stronger factors when risk signals indicate elevated threat.

**Design guidance**:
- The authentication architecture SHOULD incorporate risk signals (geographic anomaly, device change, time of access, behavioral pattern deviation) to trigger step-up authentication requirements
- Risk-based authentication decisions SHALL be logged with the triggering signals to support audit and incident investigation
- Continuous re-authentication triggers SHALL be defined for sensitive operations within an authenticated session (e.g., sensitive data export, privileged operation execution)
- Risk scoring SHOULD not be the sole determinant for reducing MFA requirements; it MAY be used to streamline MFA for low-risk, known-good contexts
page_texts.13:
[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-MFA-2.2.04.md#re-authentication-and-session-context]

#### Re-Authentication and Session Context

**Architectural intent**: Define the architectural requirements for periodic re-authentication that maintain assurance currency throughout session lifecycles, preventing stale session credentials from granting access to sensitive operations.

**Design guidance**:
- Re-authentication SHALL be required when the current session AAL is insufficient for the target resource
- Re-authentication intervals SHALL be defined per sensitivity tier; privileged sessions SHOULD require more frequent re-authentication than standard sessions
- Forced re-authentication triggers SHALL include: explicit session timeout, risk score threshold breach, sensitivity elevation (accessing higher-classification data), and administrative session revocation events
- Re-authentication SHOULD NOT require users to repeat the full authentication ceremony; supplemental factor verification SHOULD be sufficient where the primary identity claim remains valid

### Integration Interfaces

| Interface | Direction | Consuming ABB | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| AAL Signal | Outbound | GUID-SEC-IAM-IDENTITY-BROKER-2.2.02 | Authentication Assurance Level achieved, informing FAL mapping and access decision at the broker |
| Step-Up Request | Inbound | GUID-SEC-IAM-SSO-2.2.03 | Request from SSO layer to elevate authentication assurance within an active session |
| Proofing Assurance | Inbound | GUID-SEC-IAM-PROOFING-2.2.05 | Identity assurance level from proofing process, used to gate authenticator enrollment eligibility |
| MFA Event | Outbound | Enterprise SIEM | Authentication attempt, success, failure, and step-up events forwarded for monitoring and anomaly detection |
| Risk Signal | Inbound | Risk/UBA platform | Contextual risk score and anomaly signals consumed to trigger adaptive authentication |

[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-MFA-2.2.04.md#zero-trust-alignment-nist-sp-800-207]

### Zero Trust Alignment (NIST SP 800-207)

- **Identity Pillar**: MFA is the primary mechanism by which identity claims are strengthened beyond single-factor assertions; phishing-resistant MFA eliminates the class of credential interception attacks that undermine identity-based trust decisions
- **Devices Pillar**: Platform authenticators (Windows Hello for Business, Touch ID) bind authentication to specific enrolled devices, incorporating device identity into the authentication signal
- **Networks Pillar**: MFA enforcement is explicitly network-independent; internal network location SHALL NOT reduce MFA requirements, consistent with Zero Trust principles
- **Applications Pillar**: Per-application AAL requirements ensure that applications declare and enforce the authentication assurance commensurate with their sensitivity, enabling granular Zero Trust verification at the application layer

page_texts.16:
[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-MFA-2.2.04.md#nist-sp-800-53-intent-alignment]

### NIST SP 800-53 Intent Alignment

| Control Family | Architectural Intent |
|---|---|
| **IA — Identification and Authentication** | This ABB directly addresses the full intent of the IA family — requiring MFA for both organizational and privileged users, managing authenticator lifecycle, and establishing re-authentication requirements |
| **AC — Access Control** | Authenticator assurance levels and step-up architecture support the access enforcement intent of the AC family by conditioning resource access on verified, current authentication strength |
| **SC — System and Communications Protection** | Phishing-resistant authenticators (FIDO2/WebAuthn) use cryptographic binding that supports the SC family's intent for secure communications protection against interception and replay |
| **AU — Audit and Accountability** | Authentication event logging (attempts, successes, failures, step-up events) supports the AU family's intent for audit event generation and accountability |

[strategy/guidance/security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-MFA-2.2.04.md#constraints-and-dependencies]

### Constraints and Dependencies

- **Identity Proofing Dependency**: Secure authenticator enrollment depends on identity proofing (GUID-SEC-IAM-PROOFING-2.2.05); the strength of the enrollment binding is bounded by the rigor of the proofing process
- **Application Integration**: MFA enforcement at the Identity Broker or IdP layer protects applications that support federation; applications with local authentication that are not integrated with enterprise SSO require application-level MFA controls until migrated
- **Authenticator Accessibility**: FIDO2/WebAuthn phishing-resistant authenticators require hardware support (USB port, NFC, or platform TPM); accessibility accommodations must be defined for users and devices that cannot support preferred authenticator types
- **Legacy System Constraints**: Some legacy systems may not support modern authenticator integration; these systems require compensating controls and a documented migration timeline
- **Recovery Pathway Risk**: Authenticator recovery procedures represent an inherent weakening of the security model; recovery pathways MUST require identity re-verification and SHALL NOT allow recovery by social engineering of helpdesk personnel
